Qualified wellbeing practitioners provide short-term therapeutic support for young people with mild to moderate mental health and emotional wellbeing needs. You need to meet at least two of: living in Brent, having a GP in Brent, and attending school in Brent. The service supports 5 to 18 year olds, or young people up to age 25 if they have a special educational need or are disabled. You can refer yourself, but parents/carers and professionals can make referrals too.

Summary text: LYRA is a service that links together NHS teams and charities in Brent. It offers initial assessments to young people (aged up to 18, or 25 if they have a special educational need or are disabled), and then makes sure they’re referred on to the right service(s) to help them, which could include CAMHS and/or another organisation or service. LYRA doesn't provide talking therapy, but the people who work there can refer you on to the best organisation to provide therapy for you. You can refer yourself to LYRA by calling or emailing the CNWL single point of access.

A helpline that gives advice and support to people with a learning disability and their families and carers. They can advise on things like social care, safeguarding, benefits, and housing. They are not a crisis service.
A helpline giving advice and support on issues that matter to disabled people and their families. They can help with things like benefits, social care, housing, equipment, and working.

Information and support for anyone who is struggling with their eating – you do not need a formal diagnosis to get in touch. An advisor will work with you to make an action plan, and direct you towards information and support that will help you (or your lived one) work towards recovery. Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland have different phone numbers and email addresses, listed on the Beat website.

Service name: Kids Can Achieve support for SEND
Summary text: Kids Can Achieve has a family service that provides free one-to-one and group support to the parents and carers of children with a special educational need or disability. Your parents or carers can get help with things like benefits, housing, and emotional support – you don’t need a diagnosis. If you have a learning disability, your family might be able to get a small grant too. Kids Can Achieve also runs clubs and activities in Harrow, but these cost money – they can help you work out if the council or NHS can help you pay for you.

The youth hub provides lots of different activities including youth clubs, cooking sessions, gym sessions, a games night, and the Harrow Youth Parliament. Sessions are held in a few different places and have different age limits. Sometimes you can drop in, but sometimes you need to book over the phone. The youth hub also runs mental toughness sessions, but you need to be referred before you can go to these.

Empower offers young people who are struggling with their mental health weekly sessions for three months. Each session has 60 minutes of sport, followed by a 30-minute wellbeing workshop. You do not need a diagnosis, but Empower is only for people who are struggling with their wellbeing. A parent or carer can refer you.
